# Source 123 — CRS: Regulating Artificial Intelligence: U.S. and International Approaches and Considerations for Congress (R48555)

- **URL:** https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48555
- **Publisher:** Congressional Research Service (Library of Congress)
- **Author:** Laurie Harris
- **Published:** 2025-06-04 (Version 4)
- **Type:** Congressional Research Service report (nonpartisan analysis)
- **Status:** fetched 2026-09-14 (full text via exa, http 200)

## Key claims (as stated in source)
- **No federal legislation establishing broad regulatory authorities** for AI development/use or AI prohibitions has been enacted; recent Congresses have passed primarily more targeted AI provisions.
- The focus on AI safety under the Biden Administration "appears to be shifting toward security concerns during the second Trump Administration."
- Most US regulatory efforts center on (1) federal agency assessment/enforcement of existing authorities, (2) exploring whether agencies need additional authorities, and (3) securing voluntary industry commitments. Much proposed legislation (118th/119th Congresses) emphasizes voluntary guidelines/best practices and reporting of industry-conducted evaluations.
- The US federal approach "appears to be cautious in regard to regulating AI in the private sector and more focused on oversight of federal government uses of AI." In the absence of federal AI regulations, **states have been enacting their own laws**; critics say the patchwork creates compliance challenges.
- **International comparison:**
  - **UK:** measured approach (to date).
  - **EU:** broad regulatory approach via the **EU AI Act**, classifying AI systems into risk categories with different requirements/obligations; some analysts raise concerns it creates barriers for companies.
  - **China:** targeted AI laws, working on broader regulation; heavy government role in private-sector development. China's approach characterized as a **vertical, technology-specific framework** influenced by national security and economic development goals; the EU AI Act described as a **horizontal, risk-based framework** focused on ethics and transparency.
- **Policy considerations/options for Congress:** leverage existing frameworks; create new AI regulations/authorities; support US AI development/deployment; engage with international efforts. Approaches can focus on safety, security, or accelerating innovation (with voluntary commitments), or combine them.
- Report scope excludes AI infrastructure/equipment (chips, data centers) and export controls (see CRS In Focus IF12899).
- **Defining AI:** no single agreed definition; cites the National AI Initiative Act of 2020 definition ("a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments...").

## Verification notes
- Consistent with draft.md usage (CRS R48555, June 2025, US vs international AI regulation comparison).
- Primary nonpartisan CRS report — authoritative.
- The EU "horizontal, risk-based" vs China "vertical, technology-specific" characterization is the report's framing of the two regimes.
